alt: A timeline: the Universal Declaration 1948, referred to in the preamble; the Convention signed in Rome on 4 November 1950; in force on 3 September 1953. A bar shows its structure: Article 1 (obligation to respect rights), Section I Articles 2 to 18 (rights and general provisions), Section II Articles 19 to 51 (the Court) and Section III Articles 52 to 59 (miscellaneous).
caption: Rights sit in Section I; the Court takes up most of the text in Section II.

after: ## Article 1: whom does the Convention protect?
alt: States must secure the rights to everyone within their jurisdiction: citizens, foreign nationals, prisoners and asylum seekers. Jurisdiction is primarily territorial but can reach abroad where a state exercises authority and control, as in Al-Skeini v UK, where the UK had jurisdiction over civilians killed by British soldiers in Basra.
caption: Jurisdiction is mainly territorial, but follows authority and control abroad.

alt: A grid of Articles 2 to 14: life, torture, slavery, liberty, fair trial, no punishment without law, private life, religion, expression, assembly, marriage, effective remedy and discrimination. Articles 2, 5, 8, 10 and 11, the specification focus, are highlighted.
caption: The specification’s five Articles sit among thirteen in Section I.

alt: Three bands. Absolute rights, with no exceptions or balancing: Article 3, Article 4.1 and Article 7. Limited rights, where the Article lists the only exceptions: Article 2 (2.2) and Article 5 (5.1(a) to (f)). Qualified rights, with restrictions in a second paragraph: Articles 8, 9, 10 and 11.
caption: The structure of each Article tells you how far it can be restricted.

after: ## General provisions that affect every right
alt: Cards for the general Articles: 13 effective remedy, 14 discrimination (not free-standing), 16 political activity of aliens, 17 abuse of rights, 18 improper purposes. Article 15 allows derogation in war or a public emergency, but never from Article 2 (except lawful acts of war), Article 3, Article 4.1 or Article 7; the UK used it after Brogan and after 11 September 2001, quashed in A v Home Secretary.
caption: Article 15 allows derogation, but never from the core four.

alt: Protocols grouped by status. Ratified by the UK: Protocol 1 (property, education, elections), Protocol 6 and Protocol 13 (death penalty). Not ratified: Protocol 4 (freedom of movement) and Protocol 12 (free-standing discrimination). Procedural: Protocol 11 (single full-time Court), Protocol 14 (filtering and admissibility) and Protocol 15 (margin of appreciation in the preamble, four-month time limit).
caption: Some protocols add rights the UK has not accepted; others reshape the Court.

alt: A stepped pyramid of the Court’s formations: single judges filter inadmissible cases, committees of three decide well-established case law, chambers of seven decide most others, and a Grand Chamber of 17 hears the most important cases. Applications come from states (Article 33) or victims (Article 34); judgments may award just satisfaction (Article 41), bind states (Article 46) and are supervised by the Committee of Ministers.
caption: Four formations, from single-judge filtering to the Grand Chamber of 17.
